title: Points, Ticks & P&L
hook: Before you worry about making money, you need to understand how the numbers work.

launchpad.outcome: Calculate a trade's dollar P&L from points, tick value, and contract count, for wins and losses.
launchpad.missionQuestion: If someone tells you they made "50 points today," do you actually know how much money that is?

markers.label: Wins and losses scale the same

slides.body: A point is a whole-number move in price, on MNQ, 20,000 → 20,001 is 1 point. A tick is the minimum increment inside that: MNQ's tick is 0.25 points, worth $0.50 per contract, so a full point is $2.00 per contract. Tick size and value differ by contract, so don't assume every product works like MNQ.

check.prompt: A trader says: "I only have a 30-point stop, so I can't lose that much."

options.label: Nothing's missing
options.body: 30 points is 30 points, the risk is already clear.
options.feedback: Points alone don't tell you the dollar risk, you need the point value and contract count too.

options.label: Something's missing
options.body: The number of contracts and the contract's point value: points alone don't tell you the dollar risk.
options.why: Bingo. 30 points means very different things at 1 contract versus 10.

slides.title: Build your own P&L
slides.body: Points moved × point value × number of contracts. Same chart, same move, different position size, different P&L.

slides.quote: Points describe price movement. Contracts determine how much exposure you have to that movement. Never discuss risk in points alone without understanding what those points mean in dollars for your position.

slides.body: Same formula, every time: points moved × point value × contracts.

check.prompt: You buy 1 MNQ at 20,000. Price rises to 20,010, that's 10 points. What's the P&L before fees?

options.feedback: That's just the points, you still need to multiply by the point value.
That's 10x too much, check your multiplication.

slides.body: Favorable direction still multiplies out the same, whichever way you're positioned.

check.prompt: You short 2 MNQ at 20,000. Price falls to 19,985, a 15-point favorable move. What's the P&L before fees?

options.feedback: That's only 1 contract's worth, you have 2.
That's just the points, not multiplied by point value or contracts.

slides.kicker: Not every trade is a winner
slides.body: The formula doesn't care about direction, it just multiplies. A loss scales exactly the same way a gain does.

check.prompt: You buy 3 MNQ. Price moves 10 points against you. What's the P&L before fees?

options.feedback: That's only 1 contract's worth, you have 3.

options.why: 10 points × $2 × 3 contracts = $60 lost, and not every trade is a winner.

options.feedback: Check your multiplication: points × point value × contracts.

slides.body: Converting between points and ticks works the same way, multiply.

check.prompt: If 1 point = 4 ticks, how many ticks are in 2 points?

options.label: 4 ticks
options.feedback: That's ticks for just 1 point, you need 2 points' worth.

slides.prompt: Imagine another AGHF member asks: "My friend said she made 50 points today, is that a lot of money?" How would you explain it to them?
slides.modelAnswer: Points alone don't tell you anything, you need to know the instrument's point value and how many contracts she was holding. 50 points on MNQ with 1 contract is $100. 50 points on MNQ with 10 contracts is $1,000. Same 50 points, completely different amount of money.

takeaways: A point is a whole-number move; a tick is the smallest increment inside it.
P&L = points moved × point value × contract count, for wins and losses alike.
Points alone never tell you the real dollar risk, contracts and point value do.
remember: Never discuss risk in points alone.
